label: Most multiway systems grow exponentially or not at all
claim: Most multiway systems (which keep all sequences produced by all possible replacements at each step) either grow exponentially fast or do not grow at all; slow growth is rare.
quote: most either grow exponentially quickly, or not at all; slow growth of the kind seen on the facing page is rather rare.
scope: multiway (non-deterministic string rewriting) systems with simple rules

label: Slowly growing multiway systems eventually become repetitive
claim: Even when slowly growing multiway systems show early apparent randomness in their state counts, they typically end up showing some form of repetition (sometimes with long periods, such as 1071 steps).
quote: even when such growth leads to a certain amount of apparent randomness it typically in the end seems to exhibit some form of repetition.
scope: slowly growing multiway systems

label: Multiway systems build their own network of connections in time
claim: Because each sequence in a multiway system always leads to the same successors, the evolution can be represented as a network of which state leads to which, so multiway systems build up their own, often complicated, pattern of connections in time.
quote: multiway systems can in effect build up their own pattern of connections in time—and this pattern can often be quite complicated.
scope: multiway systems

label: One-dimensional local constraints can always be met by a repetitive pattern
claim: In one dimension, any set of local constraints on cell colors that can be satisfied at all can be satisfied by a simple, purely repetitive arrangement, so simple 1D constraints cannot force complex patterns.
quote: in one dimension it is possible to prove that any local set of constraints that can be satisfied at all can always be satisfied by some simple and purely repetitive arrangement of colors.
scope: one-dimensional local constraint systems (one-dimensional subshifts of finite type)

label: All satisfiable 2D nearest-neighbor template constraints allow repetitive patterns
claim: Of all 4,294,967,296 two-dimensional constraints defined by allowed templates of a cell and its four neighbors, 766,979,044 cannot be satisfied, and every one of the rest can be satisfied by a repetitive pattern, with 171 repetitive patterns sufficing for all.
quote: among the 3,527,988,252 that remain, it turns out that every single one can be satisfied by a simple repetitive pattern.
scope: two-dimensional two-color constraints on five-cell (von Neumann) neighborhood templates

label: Constraint systems require going outside the system to find their patterns
claim: Unlike rule-based systems, which can be run directly, systems defined by constraints offer no direct procedure for finding the patterns they allow; one must search from outside the system, which can take enormous computational effort.
quote: But in a system that is based on constraints, there is no such direct procedure, and instead one must in effect always go outside of the system to work out what patterns can occur.
scope: systems defined by constraints versus explicit evolution rules

label: The simplest constraint forcing a non-repetitive pattern forces a nested one
claim: Among 2D template constraints that also require one template to appear somewhere, systematic search over more than 18 million constraints finds that the first constraint forcing a non-repetitive pattern (number 18762389) forces a unique nested pattern.
quote: after examining more than 18 million of them, one finally discovers the system shown on the facing page. And in this system, unlike all others before it, no repetitive pattern is possible; the only pattern that satisfies the constraint is the non-repetitive nested pattern shown in the picture.
scope: two-dimensional template constraints with a required-template condition

label: No tested simple template constraint forces more than nested behavior
claim: Of the 137,438,953,472 template constraints with a required-template condition, none of the millions tested forces anything more complicated than nested behavior.
quote: of the millions of these that I have tested, none have forced anything more complicated than the kind of nested behavior seen on the previous page.
scope: two-dimensional template constraints with a required-template condition

label: 3x3 template constraints can force a rule 30–like random pattern
claim: Constraints on 3×3 blocks of cells can be constructed to force complex patterns: a set of 56 allowed templates forces a unique, largely random pattern equivalent to the evolution of the rule 30 cellular automaton.
quote: a system with 56 allowed templates in which the only pattern satisfying the constraint is a complex and largely random one, derived from the rule 30 cellular automaton.
scope: two-dimensional constraints on 3×3 neighborhoods

label: Simple constraints rarely force complex behavior, unlike simple rules
claim: Unlike simple evolution rules, almost all simple constraints lead only to fairly simple patterns; complex behavior forced by constraints is rare.
quote: it seems that almost all simple constraints lead only to fairly simple patterns.
scope: constraint-based systems compared with rule-based simple programs

label: Constraint-like equations helped hide complexity from traditional science
claim: Because describing complex behavior with constraints requires fairly complicated constraints, the traditional focus of science and mathematics on equations that act like constraints is another reason they failed to identify the phenomenon of complexity.
quote: the fact that traditional science and mathematics tends to concentrate on equations that operate like constraints provides yet another reason for their failure to identify the fundamental phenomenon of complexity that I discuss in this book.
scope: methods of traditional science and mathematics

label: Simple systems self-organize from random initial conditions
claim: Many simple-rule systems such as cellular automata, when started from completely random initial conditions, spontaneously organize themselves and produce behavior with many distinctly non-random features.
quote: many systems spontaneously tend to organize themselves, so that even with completely random initial conditions they end up producing behavior that has many features that are not at all random.
scope: cellular automata and similar simple programs started from random initial conditions

label: Cellular automaton behavior falls into four basic classes
claim: Despite differing in detail for almost every rule, the patterns produced by cellular automata of all kinds from random initial conditions can almost always be easily assigned to one of just four classes: uniform final state (class 1), simple stable or periodic structures (class 2), apparently random behavior (class 3), and interacting localized structures (class 4).
quote: among all kinds of cellular automata, it seems that the patterns which arise can almost always be assigned quite easily to one of just four basic classes illustrated below.
scope: all kinds of cellular automata evolved from random initial conditions

label: Class 4 consists of simple localized structures interacting in complex ways
claim: Class 4 cellular automata mix order and randomness: they produce localized structures that are individually fairly simple, but which move around and interact with each other in very complicated ways.
quote: class 4 involves a mixture of order and randomness: localized structures are produced which on their own are fairly simple, but these structures move around and interact with each other in very complicated ways.
scope: class 4 cellular automata

label: Detailed cellular automaton properties correlate with the four classes
claim: Most detailed properties of cellular automata correlate closely with the four visually defined classes, so that knowing a cellular automaton's class is often enough to predict its detailed properties.
quote: most of these properties were closely correlated with the classes that I had already identified. Indeed, in trying to predict detailed properties of a particular cellular automaton, it was often enough just to know what class the cellular automaton was in.
scope: cellular automata in general

label: A cellular automaton's class usually cannot be read off its rule
claim: For most cellular automata there is no easy way to determine from the underlying rule which class of behavior it will produce; one generally has to run it and see, though some rule forms can be shown to give only class 1 or 2 behavior.
quote: In most cases there is no easy way to do this, and in fact there is little choice but just to run the cellular automaton and see what it does.
scope: predicting cellular automaton behavior class from rule specification

label: Class 4 lies between class 2 and class 3 in activity
claim: Although class 4 is the most complex in appearance, in terms of overall activity it is intermediate between class 2 and class 3, and in sequences of rules it commonly appears at the transition between class 2 and class 3 rules.
quote: Class 4 systems are then in the middle: for the activity that they show neither dies out completely, as in class 2, nor remains at the high level seen in class 3.
scope: sequences of cellular automaton rules, both discrete and continuous

label: Continuous cellular automata show the same four classes
claim: Cellular automata whose cells take continuous gray-level values show essentially the same four classes of behavior as discrete cellular automata, with class 4 behavior and its discrete localized structures typically appearing at transitions as the rule parameter is varied.
quote: But it seems that this behavior falls into essentially the same four classes that we have already seen in ordinary cellular automata.
scope: continuous cellular automata with a smoothly varying rule parameter

label: Two-dimensional cellular automata show the same four classes
claim: Two-dimensional cellular automata exhibit the same four classes of behavior as one-dimensional ones, which becomes evident when one-dimensional slices through their evolution are examined; class 4 behavior, as in the Game of Life, occurs even on a white background with slightly more complicated rules.
quote: Indeed, by looking at such slices one can readily identify the very same four classes of behavior as in one-dimensional cellular automata.
scope: two-dimensional cellular automata

label: The four classes respond differently to small changes in initial conditions
claim: Changing one cell of the initial condition has characteristically different effects by class: in class 1 the change dies out, in class 2 it stays localized, in class 3 it spreads at a uniform rate to affect the whole system, and in class 4 it spreads only sporadically.
quote: In class 1, changes always die out, and in fact exactly the same final state is reached regardless of what initial conditions were used. In class 2, changes may persist, but they always remain localized in a small region of the system.
scope: cellular automata of all four classes

label: Natural systems can be understood by how they handle information
claim: Some of the most important features of natural systems can often be understood just by identifying which cellular automaton class their handling of information (forgetting, localized retention, long-range communication) corresponds to.
quote: it is often possible to understand some of the most important features of systems that occur in nature just by looking at how their handling of information corresponds to what we have seen in the basic classes of systems that we have identified here.
scope: natural systems in general

label: Class 2 repetitiveness stems from lack of long-range communication
claim: Class 2 cellular automata are always eventually repetitive because their lack of long-range communication makes each part behave as an independent system of limited size, typically only a few cells across, and hence with short repetition periods.
quote: the absence of long-range communication effectively forces each part of a class 2 system to behave as if it were a system of limited size.
section: Systems of Limited Size and Class 2 Behavior
scope: class 2 cellular automata

label: Finite discrete deterministic systems must eventually repeat
claim: Any system of limited size made of discrete elements and following definite rules must eventually exhibit repetitive behavior, with repetition period at most equal to its total number of possible states.
quote: it is then a general result that any system of limited size that involves discrete elements and follows definite rules must always eventually exhibit repetitive behavior.
section: Systems of Limited Size and Class 2 Behavior
scope: finite-state deterministic discrete systems

label: Repetition periods of class 3 rules grow rapidly with system size
claim: In cellular automata on a finite cyclic lattice, a rapid increase of repetition period with lattice size is characteristic of class 3 behavior, with large fluctuations as size changes; among elementary rules only rule 45 appears to give periods always near the maximum possible.
quote: In general, a rapid increase with size is characteristic of class 3 behavior. Of the elementary rules, however, only rule 45 seems to yield periods that always stay close to the maximum of 2^n.
section: Systems of Limited Size and Class 2 Behavior
scope: elementary cellular automata on cyclic lattices of size n

label: Class 3 randomness can arise without randomness in initial conditions
claim: The randomness of class 3 systems is not merely inherited from random initial conditions: random behavior can be generated even when the initial conditions contain no randomness at all.
quote: the crucial point that I discovered only some time later is that random behavior can also occur even when there is no randomness in initial conditions.
scope: class 3 cellular automata such as rule 30 and rule 22

label: Additive rule 90 only transmits randomness from its initial conditions
claim: Because rule 90 is additive, its patterns are superpositions of the single-cell nested pattern, so it cannot generate randomness intrinsically; any randomness it shows comes from the initial conditions, and deviations such as a low initial density persist forever, unlike in rule 22.
quote: In rule 22 the low initial density has no long-term effect. But in rule 90 its effect continues forever.
scope: additive cellular automata (rule 90) versus non-additive class 3 rules (rule 22)

label: Intrinsic randomness generation makes large-scale behavior stable
claim: Systems that intrinsically generate randomness, like rule 22 or rule 30, produce the same overall random behavior with the same large-scale properties whatever their initial conditions, giving them a fundamental stability that he says underlies the apparent stability of many systems in nature.
quote: By intrinsically generating randomness such systems in a sense have a certain fundamental stability: for whatever is done to their initial conditions, they still give the same overall random behavior, with the same large-scale properties.
scope: intrinsically random cellular automata and natural systems with apparent stability

label: Spatially periodic initial conditions always give repetitive behavior
claim: In any cellular automaton, an initial condition consisting of a fixed block of n cells repeated forever leads to repetitive behavior with period at most 2^n, since each block evolves like a finite cyclic system.
quote: in any cellular automaton it is inevitable that initial conditions which consist just of a fixed block of cells repeated forever will lead to simple repetitive behavior.
scope: all cellular automata with spatially periodic initial conditions

label: Special initial conditions often make one cellular automaton emulate another
claim: It is common for a cellular automaton to have special initial conditions under which it behaves exactly like some other cellular automaton; for example rule 126 behaves like rule 90 when started from paired-cell blocks, and class 3 rules can thereby act like class 2 rules.
quote: it turns out to be quite common for there to exist special initial conditions for one cellular automaton that make it behave just like some other cellular automaton.
scope: cellular automata and their block emulations

label: Nested patterns arise from rules that emulate themselves
claim: A cellular automaton whose blocks of cells evolve by the same rule as individual cells must produce patterns that are either essentially uniform or nested; this self-emulation is why rule 90 and rules that emulate it produce nested patterns.
quote: And this can be achieved in only two ways: either the pattern must be essentially uniform, or it must have a nested structure—just like we see in rule 90.
scope: self-emulating cellular automata

label: Additive rules self-emulate; rules 90 and 150 are the only elementary ones
claim: Every additive cellular automaton rule can emulate itself and therefore yields nested patterns, and among two-color nearest-neighbor rules the only fundamentally different additive rules are rules 90 and 150; self-emulation is otherwise rare, though non-additive examples such as rule 184 exist.
quote: one can show that any rule that is additive will be able to emulate itself and will thus yield nested patterns. But there are rather few additive rules, and indeed with two colors and nearest neighbors the only fundamentally different ones are precisely rules 90 and 150.
scope: additive cellular automata, especially elementary rules

label: Allowed-sequence networks grow fast for class 3 and 4, slowly for 1 and 2
claim: As cellular automata evolve, the set of cell sequences that can occur generally becomes progressively restricted; the finite networks describing these sets stay simple (about t^2 nodes after t steps) for class 1 and 2 rules but grow at least exponentially for most class 3 and 4 rules, apart from surjective rules started from all possible sequences.
quote: Indeed, this kind of rapid increase in network complexity is a general characteristic of most class 3 and 4 rules.
scope: one-dimensional cellular automata and the regular languages of their configurations

label: Class 4 systems always have structures that persist forever
claim: A crucial feature of any class 4 cellular automaton is that, although most structures that form eventually die out, there must always be certain structures that can persist forever in it.
quote: Most of these structures eventually die out, sometimes in rather complicated ways. But a crucial feature of any class 4 systems is that there must always be certain structures that can persist forever in it.
scope: class 4 cellular automata

label: Complicated persistent structures imply moving structures exist
claim: In class 4 cellular automata, whenever sufficiently complicated persistent structures occur, structures that move can eventually be found; moving structures are what allow information to travel and complex class 4 behavior to occur.
quote: My experience with many different rules is that whenever sufficiently complicated persistent structures occur, structures that move can eventually be found.
scope: class 4 cellular automata

label: Class 4 automata can mimic many other systems
claim: Class 4 cellular automata can, with appropriate initial conditions, mimic the behavior of all sorts of other systems, including producing unbounded growth of either complex or very simple form.
quote: it is a general feature of class 4 cellular automata that with appropriate initial conditions they can mimic the behavior of all sorts of other systems.
scope: class 4 cellular automata

label: Interactions among simple structures in rule 110 give immense complexity
claim: Although individual persistent structures in class 4 systems such as rule 110 behave fairly repetitively, collisions between them can produce cascades of new structures and outcomes that take very many steps to resolve, yielding behavior of immense complexity from an extremely simple rule.
quote: So even though the individual structures in class 4 systems like rule 110 may behave in fairly repetitive ways, interactions between these structures can lead to behavior of immense complexity.
scope: rule 110 and other class 4 cellular automata

label: Universal behavior types span simple programs and natural systems
claim: The same kinds of overall behavior arise regardless of the details of underlying rules, and this universality holds not only among simple programs but also between simple programs and systems in nature, so idealized cell models and real molecular systems should show the same universal features.
quote: And the crucial point is that I believe that this universality extends not only across simple programs, but also to systems in nature.
scope: simple programs and natural systems with different underlying components

label: Just three basic mechanisms account for randomness
claim: Apparent randomness in any system arises from one of just three basic mechanisms: continual random input from the environment, randomness transcribed from initial conditions, or intrinsic generation of randomness by the system's own rules with no random input.
quote: But from my investigations of simple programs I have come to the conclusion that one can in fact identify just three basic mechanisms for randomness, as illustrated in the pictures below.
scope: all systems, natural or computational, that show apparent randomness

label: Intrinsic randomness generation explains most randomness in nature
claim: The mechanism in which a system's own deterministic rules generate randomness without any random input is ultimately responsible for a large fraction, and perhaps essentially all, of the randomness seen in the natural world.
quote: I believe that this mechanism is in fact ultimately responsible for a large fraction, if not essentially all, of the randomness that we see in the natural world.
scope: random-looking phenomena in the natural world

label: Hardware noise-based random generators deviate from perfect randomness
claim: Devices that generate randomness by amplifying microscopic environmental noise (spark gaps, vacuum tubes, semiconductor diodes) have consistently been found to produce output with significant deviations from perfect randomness, because the sampling device relaxes only gradually and because the environment itself has correlations.
quote: But despite such sensitivity to microscopic effects, what has consistently been found in practice is that the output from such devices has significant deviations from perfect randomness.
scope: physical random number generators based on electronic or other environmental noise

label: Randomness from initial conditions lasts only a limited number of steps
claim: In physical chaotic systems such as kneading, mirror arrangements or pegboards, randomness can be attributed purely to initial conditions only for a small number of steps (around ten collisions for a pegboard), because amplification quickly reaches atomic scales and environmental perturbations take over; the limit is set by the separation between observed large-scale and uncontrollable small-scale features.
quote: So the idea that randomness comes purely from initial conditions can be realistic only for a fairly small number of steps; randomness which is seen after that must therefore typically be attributed to other mechanisms.
section: Chaos Theory and Randomness from Initial Conditions
scope: physical systems with sensitive dependence on initial conditions

label: Solar system motion should show sensitive dependence over millions of years
claim: Although planetary motion looks regular on human timescales, sensitive dependence on initial conditions should ultimately occur in the solar system, producing significant randomness over a few million years that may explain some present-day features of the solar system.
quote: But calculations imply that sensitive dependence on initial conditions should ultimately occur even in our solar system.
section: Chaos Theory and Randomness from Initial Conditions
scope: orbital dynamics of planets and other bodies in the solar system

label: Maximal-period linear congruential generators still show strong nonrandomness
claim: Linear congruential random number generators designed to have maximal repetition period have repeatedly turned out to deviate substantially from perfect randomness (for example, successive outputs plotted as points fall on regular stripes), because the mathematical tractability that guarantees their period also implies regularity.
quote: But in practice over the years, one after another linear congruential generator that has been constructed to have maximal repetition period has turned out to exhibit very substantial deviations from perfect randomness.
scope: linear congruential pseudorandom number generators

label: Amenability to mathematical analysis implies deviations from randomness
claim: The very possibility of detailed mathematical analysis of a system tends to imply that its output has at least some deviations from perfect randomness, whereas simple rules not constrained by the need for such analysis can generate highly random behavior.
quote: the very possibility of any detailed mathematical analysis tends to imply the presence of at least some deviations from perfect randomness.
scope: deterministic systems used to generate randomness, including pseudorandom generators

label: Rapid production of much randomness indicates intrinsic generation
claim: Whenever a large amount of randomness is produced in a short time, intrinsic randomness generation is overwhelmingly likely to be responsible, because it uses every component of a system to produce new randomness and has no length limit, whereas environmental amplification is slow and initial-condition randomness is short-lived.
quote: The basic answer, I believe, is that whenever a large amount of randomness is produced in a short time, intrinsic randomness generation is overwhelmingly likely to be the mechanism responsible.
scope: natural and engineered systems that produce randomness

label: Intrinsically generated randomness is repeatable across experimental runs
claim: If randomness in an experiment comes from intrinsic generation, then even the precise details of the random-looking behavior should be repeatable from one run to the next, because such behavior is robust to perturbations below a critical size, whereas randomness from the environment or from initial conditions should show little or no repeatability.
quote: But what is remarkable is that if intrinsic randomness generation is the mechanism at work, then the precise details of the behavior can also be repeatable.
scope: carefully controlled experiments showing random-looking behavior
